source: CARDI (Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute) / វិទ្យាស្ថានស្រាវជ្រាវ និងអភិវឌ្ឍន៍កសិកម្មកម្ពុជា, presentation 'ផលិតកម្មគ្រាប់ពូជ គុណភាព និង ចំណាត់ថ្នាក់' (Seed Production, Quality, and Classification), prepared by Mr. Sang Laiyheng, Deputy Director of the Seed Multiplication Office (Tel: 012 952 801; Email: s_layheng@yahoo.com), dated December 1, 2014.
text:
Mixed seed (គ្រាប់ពូជលាយ) is seed that carries genetic or physical characteristics different from the target variety. Its presence in a seed lot reduces yield and quality and causes loss of the variety's original identity, so seed producers must regularly rogue (purify) fields by identifying and removing any plant or grain that differs from the required variety's characteristics. Mixed seed can be identified by inspecting the physical characteristics of the grain.

CARDI training material lists four main causes of seed mixture during production:

1. Mutation: a sudden, relatively infrequent change in the genetic makeup of a plant or grain that causes characteristics different from the parent variety to appear. Contributing factors can include sunlight, chemical substances in the soil, and insect damage.

2. Crossing (cross-pollination): although rice is normally a self-pollinating crop, cross-pollination with other rice plants growing nearby can still occur, with an outcrossing rate that depending on field conditions can reach up to about 0.02%. To prevent this in seed production fields, an isolation strip of at least 4 meters must be maintained around the seed field; rice grown in this isolation strip plays an important role in blocking pollen carried by wind from other varieties from reaching the seed crop.

3. Ratooning and volunteer plants: regrowth from cut stubble (ratoons) or volunteer plants germinating from seed left behind by a previous crop can appear in a seed production field when land preparation/plowing was not done thoroughly, contaminating the new seed crop with the previous variety.

4. Handling: every step in seed handling -- sowing, transplanting, harvesting, threshing, sun-drying, cleaning/winnowing, transport, bagging, and storage -- is a point at which seed of different varieties or lots can become mixed together if not carefully separated and controlled.

Because of these risks, CARDI guidance stresses that seed production fields should be transplanted in straight rows with only one seedling per hill (to make off-type plants easy to spot and rogue), and that field maintenance/care must be done actively and regularly throughout the season to obtain good-quality seed and high yield.
